w: Long known locally as 'The Pits', this Whetstone park sits on old gravel pits where a 1925 tragedy drowned a boy and two friends whose raft capsized. Its pond, redwoods and Cedar of Lebanon survive, and in the early 1970s its upper lawn was a Monty Python filming location.

n: Church of St Cyril of Turau and All the Patron Saints of the Belarusian People
w: The first wooden church built in London since the Great Fire, and the first purpose-built Eastern Catholic church in the city, this Woodside Park chapel is also the first Western European memorial to the 1986 Chernobyl disaster. Built chiefly from cross-laminated timber, it stands beside the Belarusian library.

_facts: First wooden church built in London since the Great Fire

n: Francis Skaryna Belarusian Library and Museum
w: The only library outside Belarus dedicated solely to Belarusian studies, formally established as an independent institution in 1971 and run by a charitable trust ever since. It stands next to the Belarusian community's own church, named for the pioneering publisher Francysk Skaryna.

w: Designed in 1754 by Isaac Ware for Admiral John Byng, this neo-Palladian house south of Potters Bar still belongs to the same family, at the centre of a 2,500-acre estate. One of the largest private houses inside the M25, its facade has appeared in filming more than 60 times, and is Grade II* listed.

n: New Barnet (East Barnet Valley) War Memorial
w: Unveiled in 1921 at the junction of Station Road and Lyonsdown Road, this Grade II listed obelisk names 277 men and one woman of the East Barnet Valley district killed in the First World War. A campaign by Catherine Loveday added 136 WWII names; a bronze winged victory tops the column.

w: Built in 1880 to a design by Peter Dollar, this Victorian Gothic house at 15 The Crescent overlooks Monken Hadley Common on New Barnet's northern edge. It was once home to comedian Spike Milligan, whose residence here remains the house's best-known claim to fame.

w: Barnet Gate Mill, also called Arkley Windmill, is a Grade II* listed tower mill at Barnet Gate in the London Borough of Barnet -- ground that was originally part of Hertfordshire. The high grade marks it as a building of exceptional interest, though there is no public access; it can only be seen from outside.

w: Grade II listed almshouses on Wood Street in Chipping Barnet, built in 1729. Nearly three centuries on, this small row of listed housing still stands on the old high street, a quiet survivor from Georgian Barnet amid later shopfronts and traffic.
s: Georgian almshouses still standing on Barnet's high street
